newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's post office sets sights on privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Italy's post office sets sights on privatisation.

text.p: Italy's Post Office, traditionally seen as unwieldy and inefficient, is planning to turn itself into a dynamic financial services provider and hopes to have a blueprint for its privatisation ready by the end of the year.
Enzo Cardi, chairman of the loss-making state body, told Reuters Financial Television that the Post Office wanted to boost its retail services ahead of a two-part sell-off.
"I hope that by the end of this year we will have a (privatisation) project submitted to the government," Cardi said.

"It's a matter of giving the government a concrete perception that there would be shareholders and that these shareholders would be strong enough to manage the system. I hope that by the autumn, before the end of the year, this project could be laid before the government," he said in English.
Italy's sometimes problematic privatisation programme is moving ahead with the third tranche sale of energy giant Eni next week.
Cardi said the Treasury, which controls the Post Office, could follow the route chosen by Germany and the Netherlands to separate letter handling from post banking operations.
"Something a little different may also be on the horizon in the sense of having (a) holding that would control a post bank and a post office company," he said.
"We suppose that this may be the way to follow in Italy so that we...would have two privatisations, the first of the post bank and the second of the post office company."

The Post Office has already started preparing for life in the marketplace. It has shed 60,000 jobs by not replacing retiring staff and now has 180,000 employees. Cardi has also pledged to return it to break-even in 1997 after a loss last year of some 800 billion lire ($470.3 million).

He said the network of 15,000 branches in even the smallest villages in Italy -- including post offices in 3,000 where there are no banks -- had successfully moved into financial services two years ago when it started offering state bonds, or BOTs.
Italians are among the most enthusiastic savers in the world, and state bonds are the favoured instrument. The Post Office also plans to sell the forthcoming Eni shares.
"At the moment we are the biggest provider of financial services in Italy," Cardi said. But he did not see the Post Office in direct competition with Italian high street banks.
"One perspective on which we are working is that banks that are now our competitors in financial services and the payment system may become our shareholders," Cardi said.

"We are not ready to take a risk position, such as a risk on credit...Our mission is to provide the role of a retail system. The banks instead can be the supplier of the products that can be sold in this retail system."

Such services include providing mortgages, personal bank loans, postal bonds and exchange services and other consumer services such as the distribution of American Express Co cards, which was announced earlier this week.

Massimo Quarra, managing director of American Express consumer services in Italy, Switzerland and Greece, told Reuters Financial Television that he had been pleasantly surprised by the dynamic spirit at the Post Office.
"I found a company that is changing, very flexible and aggressive," he said. "They have aggressive goals of privatisation and they intend to compete in the market place." ($1=1,690 lire)
